Another major difference: The "Pi" refers to specific hardware (where all models of Pi host a 32-bit ARM CPU) while "Arduino" is more of a standard software layer (read "basic C++ with standard hardware libraries") on top of a larger variety of 8-bit CPUs...often an AVR. The "Raspbian Linux O/S" that is typically installed on the Pi would be closer to what "Arduino" really is for the 8-bit boards.

Forgetting all of the other hardware differences between the two platforms, the most significant is that the heftier 32-bit ARM comes with a typical SDRAM controller, and the MMU for it needed by Linux. The 8-bitters that run Arduino instead use on-chip SRAM for their memory, and do not have an MMU. Where you can run an app on top of Linux on top of the Pi hardware, the Arduino platform is more like an app running directly on top of the 8-bit hardware, with a few libraries linked into your app to act as the hardware driver.
Add something like "Pi is good for digital, Arduino is easier for analog interfacing," and you could replace the article in question with your two paragraphs.
